newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar firmer; bonds fall on upbeat data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar firmer; bonds fall on upbeat data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rose Monday as the market recovered from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks last Wednesday about high stock prices and possibly higher interest rates.
Bonds fell and the dollar rose on upbeat economic data and as investors braced for Friday's key employment report.
The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 41.18 points to 6,918.92 after losing more than 160 points the last three sessions.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,287 to 1,211 on moderate volume of 432.6 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Greenspan's remarks still rippled through the bond market, where the 30-year Treasury bond fell 12/32, or $3.75 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.83 percent from 6.80 percent on Friday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Investors were also greeted with a rude surprise Monday when AT&T Corp. outlined plans to enter new local telephone and wireless markets that will require massive spending, eating into earnings. AT&T fell $3 to $36.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The weak bond market, coupled with AT&T's decline, made the stock market's moderate gains appear all the more impressive, analysts said.
"You had two major negatives today and the market was still able to basically reverse course," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
When buyers did emerge, they descended on the technology stocks that led the market to record highs in mid-February and lately have led it back down.
Analysts called the rebound encouraging but stopped short of predicting an end to the market's recent weakness.
"It's going to be a while before these stocks regain their luster," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co.

Analysts noted that Greenspan's scheduled appearance before the House Banking Committee on Wednesday and a key monthly employment report due on Friday would likely preclude any meaningful rise in stocks in the meantime.
The dollar climbed to 1.6970 German marks from 1.6894 late Friday. It also advanced to 121.24 Japanese yen from 120.17.
Coffee prices soared to the highest level in two years and and soybeans also rose Monday as Brazilian dockworkers prepared for a strike that could cripple exports of Brazil's most valuable crops.
Coffee for May delivery jumped 8 cents to 184.85 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, the highest level for the most active contract since March 1995.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, March soybeans hit a high of $8.12 a bushel, before closing up 14 cents at $8.05 a bushel.
Overseas, London's FTSE ended 1.2 points down at 4,307.1. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average lost 127.87 points, or 0.69 percent, to close at 18,429.13.
